newsitem.title: USA: EMU members must show can stay the course-Maystadt.
newsitem.headline: EMU members must show can stay the course-Maystadt.

text.p: Europe must decide whether countries can stick to budget discipline in the medium-term when it agrees which countries will join a single currency, Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said.
But in an interview with Reuters, he said it would be preferable for countries, notably those in the Mediterranean who fear being left out of EMU, to join.
"For many political reasons, we would prefer that Spain and Italy would be in," he said here late Tuesday at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
Plans for a budget stability pact would ensure countries stuck to long-term fiscal discipline even after the start of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.
"If all the participants agree to the stability pact, they can no longer use tricks," he said.
He noted that European Monetary Institute head Alexandre Lamfalussy had already started stressing the importance of the medium-term outlook in deciding who qualified to join EMU.
"In its report (on which countries qualify) the European Commission should take into account the medium-term perspective of the member state," he said.

His comments echoed those of other EU officials who are increasingly emphasising a Maastricht treaty provision covering the medium-term outlook to discourage countries from making an unsustainable dash to cut deficits in time.

Maystadt also said ministers had agreed nearly all points of the stability pact, in which countries will aim to keep their budgets in balance but can run deficits of up to three percent of gross domestic product during an economic slowdown.
They would be fined if they went over three percent, unless this was due to exceptional circumstances.

"In Dublin we agreed on practically everything about the stability pact. The most difficult issue is how we define exceptional circumstances which would justify countries having a deficit exceeding three percent of GDP," he said.
EU finance ministers agreed in principle at a meeting in Dublin last month on the stability pact but deferred a final decision to a summit of EU leaders in December.

Maystadt said "there was a sense of consensus" among EU finance ministers to support proposals by the European Commission which would fine countries 0.2 percent of GDP if their deficits overshot, rising according to the increase in the deficit, with a ceiling on the fine of 0.5 percent.
But it was very hard to define "exceptional circumstances". There might, for example, be natural disasters such as earthquakes, which knocked a country off course.

"We should try to define (exceptional circumstances) as precisely as possible, but I'm not sure it is possible to define exactly in advance. It's not possible to define the magnitude of disasters," he said.

Maystadt, one of the few ministers still in office who negotiated the Maastricht treaty, also said he believed countries should have been a member of the Exchange Rate Mechanism for two years prior to the start of EMU to qualify.

European officials give a range of interpretations to a Maastricht requirement for currency stability, with Britain, which was forced out of the ERM in 1992 after a currency crisis, suggesting ERM membership is not required, and others arguing that countries should have been in the ERM for two years prior to the decision in early 1998 on who joins.
If the latter argument were accepted, countries not in the ERM by June 1996 -- notably Italy which is now seeking to join -- would already be excluded.
